blindSummary:
This country pairs a legal framework now among the region's strongest for trans people with streets among the region's most dangerous. Legal gender recognition has existed since 2016; a 2024 reform law lets adults change name and sex/gender on the national ID card directly through the civil registry (one time, no surgery); and constitutional-court rulings in 2024-25 extended document changes to trans adolescents and reprimanded the legislature for stalling trans-rights implementation.

The violence side is severe: an LGBTQ advocacy organisation documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023, with inadequate state response, and a state-declared internal armed conflict against gangs has intensified general violence since January 2024 — two more LGBTQ people were killed in its first weeks. The capital and the largest city carry real street risk, and police capacity is consumed by the security crisis.

For a visitor: documents and expression are legally protected, but the probability of encountering violence if outed in public is among the highest in the region right now.
blindOutOfScope: The general security emergency affects all travellers; only the trans-specific legal and violence picture is assessed here.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): same-sex marriage legal since 2019 (adoption still barred by constitutional ban); legal gender recognition since 2016 but not available under 18; conversion practices partially prohibited, with torture-based conversion explicitly criminalised; the constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation but gender identity/expression/sex characteristics are not explicit; police and prosecutors often fail to investigate hate crimes.

A foreign government's 2011 human-rights report on this country: documents discrimination based on sexual orientation among societal problems, alongside excessive police force, media restrictions and corruption - baseline context.

A university's political-database archive: the official translation of this country's 2008 constitution - its anti-discrimination clause prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the constitutional framework underpinning LGBT rights here.

LGBTQ news outlet (May 2018): the constitutional court ordered the civil registry to register a 7-year-old girl with both mothers' surnames - a historic recognition of LGBT families; context: decriminalisation 1997, civil unions 2015, and a 2016 law allowing people to choose their preferred gender on ID cards; adoption and surrogacy gaps remain.
